title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
Scammers have impersonated Terry Gross and other NPR Fresh Air staff in emails to authors, entertainers and public figures. The fraudulent messages reference recent work by targets and propose interviews, then request hundreds of dollars for supposed production costs. WHYY and NPR confirmed they never charge guests and are investigating with law enforcement.

The impersonation succeeded because the emails were highly personalized, making them appear legitimate to recipients who initially believed they were real interview opportunities. Cybersecurity experts note that artificial intelligence is making these scams increasingly convincing compared to traditional frauds. The deployment failure was the lack of a verification step, since targets had no reliable way to confirm the sender's identity before responding to the fraudulent messages.

It is not established whether the scammers used AI to generate the personalized content, nor what specific AI systems or techniques were deployed in the fraud itself.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other NPR Fresh Air staff to defraud authors, entertainers and public figures. The fraudsters send highly personalized emails referencing the targets' recent work and proposing interviews, then request payment of hundreds of dollars for supposed production costs. Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black received such an email and initially believed it was legitimate, only to discover the scam when asked to pay $250. Similar schemes have targeted comedian Bruce Vilanch and other celebrities using the names of public figures like Katie Couric, Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler.

WHYY, NPR and Fresh Air have confirmed they never charge guests for interviews and are investigating with law enforcement. Cybersecurity experts note that artificial intelligence is making these impersonations increasingly convincing and personalized compared to traditional scams. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from Gmail addresses, and the implausibility of major show hosts personally handling booking logistics. Victims should verify suspicious interview requests by contacting the organization directly through legitimate channels rather than responding to the fraudulent messages.
